rv.q: “Scene Partners,” by John J. Caswell Jr., with the transcendent Dianne Wiest as Meryl, is definitely more like whoa.
If the experience isn’t always fully rewarding, it’s consistently intriguing.
Scene Partners is just additional proof that that love was justified.
Discombobulation, to put it mildly, is a state of mind that Wiest conveys with enormous ease.

But too often he jumbles the poignant story within an inch of its life, trying out dozens of postmodernisms in an effort to explain one woman’s profound tragedy through the last century of American pop phenomena.
Scene Partners may be negligible, but it is a welcome opportunity to savor the two-time Oscar-winning Ms. Wiest’s tremendous talent onstage as Meryl Kowalski.
But the solid production can’t completely compensate for the elusiveness of the script.
But the pieces of his collage don’t come together.
Dianne Wiest stars in John J Caswell Jr’s murky story of a woman on a path to self-discovery – that may or may not all be a fantasy
But it’s all kind of incoherent — narratively, structurally, tonally.
After 100 lethargic minutes of Scene Partners, it’s unlikely you’ll care one way or another.
Caswell has crafted a truly engaging, enervating piece of theater.
Indeed, it’s a treat to see the two-time Oscar winner command the stage as a 75-year-old frump from the Midwest who impulsively decides to move to Hollywood in search of film stardom circa 1985.
It plays with the head, in both an engaging and disassociating manner that works, and doesn't.
Scene Partners has less structure to hold on to, and a penchant for fast pivots, leaving its audience to tumble out of the theater off-balance.
The writing here feels too clever by half.

cn.t: Wiest's magnetic performance anchors Caswell's ambitious but bewildering meta-theatrical puzzle about an elderly woman chasing Hollywood dreams. Critics are divided: some embrace its playful absurdism, while others find it messy and self-indulgent.
